Title: September 10, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session - 2027 Recommended Budget

Topic1.Title: Opening Remarks and City Manager Introduction of 2027 Recommended Budget
Topic1.Summary: Council Member Adams opened the study session and outlined the meeting format, with staff presentation followed by questions and council discussion. City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermark introduced the 2027 recommended budget, describing it as shaped by hard trade-offs, department input, and evolving outcomes-based budgeting practices. She highlighted new tools including the Budget at a Glance page and a service inventory categorizing services into five tiers. She noted that community priorities such as wildfire, climate risk, policing, housing, and wellness informed the proposal. CFO Christa Morrison then framed the budget as the third consecutive year of reductions driven by slowing revenues and rising costs.

Topic2.Title: 2027 Recommended Budget Overview and Revenue Forecast
Topic2.Summary: Budget Officer Charlotte Husky presented a total budget of $552.6 million, including a $412.2 million (later cited as $417.2 million) operating budget with roughly 2.3% growth and a $135.4 million capital budget. The city faced a projected $6.3 million general fund gap, addressed through ongoing reductions, realignments, and limited enhancements. Sales and use tax, which comprises about 35% of city revenues, is projected to grow 3.3%, while property tax is expected to rise 6%. New revenues include a $3 million transportation maintenance fee, a recreational marijuana tax increase from 3.5% to 5.5%, and utility fee increases. Revenue remains highly restricted, with a large share of funds dedicated to specific uses.

Topic3.Title: Fund Our Future Community Engagement
Topic3.Summary: Staff reported that the Fund Our Future community conversations engaged over 500 residents through in-person and online trade-off exercises across 25 services grouped into 12 categories. Community priorities included ongoing maintenance of city facilities, public safety, wildfire resilience, and affordable housing. Engagement results were used as a key pillar in budget decision-making. Staff emphasized that residents had to choose between service areas, reflecting the difficulty of balancing demand against constrained resources.

Topic4.Title: Operating Budget Changes by Sustainability, Equity, and Resilience Goal Area
Topic4.Summary: Principal Budget Analyst Scott Carpenter reviewed major operating changes, including a $4.3 million increase for facilities maintenance and wildfire-related investments of about $11 million citywide. Public safety changes included three new police lieutenant positions and firefighter equipment replacement, while affordable housing investments included $5.3 million for the Alpine Balsam site and funding for other projects. Reductions included Spruce Pool operating support (funded with one-time dollars through 2027), elimination of child watch at East Boulder Community Center, and a shoulder-season reduction at Scott Carpenter Pool. A new Office of Customer Experience and a statistically valid community survey budgeted at $150,000 were also included.

Topic5.Title: Capital Improvement Program 2027-2032 and Long-Term Financial Strategy
Topic5.Summary: Budget Officer Husky presented a $135.4 million 2027 capital budget and $827.7 million six-year CIP across seven departments, with roughly 75% supporting utilities and transportation. Major projects include the $13.5 million Barker gravity pipeline repair, Colorado 119 bus priority signal improvements, wildfire prevention projects on open space, and replacement of Fire Stations 2 and 4 totaling $31.7 million. The CIP also includes $27.9 million in facilities maintenance funded by the Community, Culture, Resilience and Safety tax. Staff described the long-term financial strategy, with a comprehensive financial plan expected in winter or December 2026, and noted a November 2026 recreation and safety bond on the ballot.

Topic6.Title: Council Questions, Process, and Budget Amendment Timeline
Topic6.Summary: Council members asked about the Alpine Balsam project's costs, facility reserve funding under the 2 percent CRV policy, fixed-term positions, property tax assessment changes, and the mechanism for substantive changes. Staff clarified that proposed amendments must be submitted by September 28, 2026, must include an identified offset, and will be considered at the October 1 first reading, with final adoption on October 15. Staff also explained that the city has an internal auditor and that the Spruce Pool, pool fees, and day services center funding will need ongoing solutions. Council members raised questions on wildfire funding, snow and ice removal, photo enforcement elimination, grant pursuit, and the lack of a statistically valid survey. Some council members proposed reallocations, including a roughly $2 million to $4 million shift toward wildfire mitigation.
